crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Curriculum and Learning Outcomes
children.blurb: Curriculum and learning outcomes define what a course or program expects learners to know, do, and value by the end of instruction.

children.name: Generating Assessments
children.blurb: Generating assessments covers the creation of test items, question banks, rubrics, distractors, and formative checks aligned to learning objectives.

children.name: Personalised Learning and Early Warning
children.blurb: Personalised learning and early warning covers systems that adapt content, pace, or feedback to individual learners and that flag students at risk of falling behind or dropping out.

children.name: Course-Specific AI Tutors
children.blurb: Course-specific AI tutors are software systems configured for a single course or module, drawing on that course's syllabus, readings, problem sets, and assessment criteria to answer student questions and give feedback.

children.name: Lecture Materials from Notes
children.blurb: Lecture materials from notes covers the conversion of an instructor's raw notes, marginal annotations, and outline fragments into structured teaching artifacts such as slide decks, handouts, discussion prompts, and study guides.

sections.body: Course design and teaching with AI involves using machine learning and language models to help instructors plan courses, write exam questions, adapt material to individual students, build subject-specific assistants, and turn raw notes into slides or handouts. In practice, systems now draft learning objectives from a syllabus, generate multiple choice questions from a textbook chapter, flag students whose quiz scores or login patterns suggest they may fall behind, answer student questions about a specific course's content, and convert a lecturer's rough notes into structured summaries. These are working tools, not just proposals, and some universities and training providers use them alongside human review.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The most reliable work is in generating first drafts and routine materials, such as quiz questions, summaries and slide outlines, where a human instructor still checks accuracy and tone. Personalised learning and early warning systems can identify patterns in student activity, but they are not yet dependable enough to make high-stakes decisions on their own, and they can reflect bias in the data they were trained on. Course-specific tutors can answer common questions well when the source material is clear and narrow, but they still make factual errors and can give confident wrong answers outside that material. The honest limit is that none of these systems understand teaching, they predict likely text or patterns, so every output needs professional judgement before it reaches a student.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader looking at how AI helps set goals and structure a course should start with Curriculum and Learning Outcomes, which covers mapping topics to objectives and aligning them with standards. From there, Generating Assessments shows how the same underlying models produce quizzes, rubrics and exam questions, and what to check before using them. Personalised Learning and Early Warning moves from static materials to student behaviour, explaining how systems adapt content or flag risk based on activity data. Course-Specific AI Tutors narrows the focus to assistants trained on one subject or syllabus, while Lecture Materials from Notes closes the loop by turning an instructor's own notes into usable teaching resources. Together these pages move from planning, to testing, to supporting individual students, to building a tutor, to producing the materials that tie the course together.
